name: Asaka Distillery (Sasanokawa Shuzo, Koriyama)
ja: 安積蒸溜所（笹の川酒造）
text: Whisky arm of Sasanokawa Shuzo, a sake brewery founded in 1765. Its predecessor Yamazakura Shuzo took the whisky licence in 1946; 'Cherry Whisky' sold well in the 1980s and production stopped in 1989. Pot stills were installed in 2015, the 250th anniversary, and distilling restarted in 2016. The Yamazakura brand (named after the predecessor's trade name) was released from old stock in 2014; one source says 2015.
flavor: Sources consulted give no tasting notes; the house style is presented through blends built on Asaka malt, bottled at 47%.
use: Sold as Yamazakura World Blended (Asaka malt as key malt, 47%) and as Asaka-distilled single releases; a sake-brewery whisky from Tohoku.
craft: Check the label: Yamazakura bottlings from the 2014 stock era and blends that include imported whisky differ from pure Asaka-distilled spirit. Release year of the brand is given as 2014 or 2015 depending on the source, so verify with the maker.

name: Nagahama Distillery (AMAHAGAN)
text: One of Japan's smallest whisky distilleries, run by Nagahama Roman Beer in Nagahama, Shiga, and operating since November 2016. Motto 'one brew, one cask': each batch yields about 200-250 litres of new make and roughly 350 batches are run a year. Two wash stills and one spirit still of alembic type with narrow necks. Water is Mt. Ibuki snowmelt. Brands: Single Malt Nagahama, Single Cask Nagahama and AMAHAGAN.
flavor: Narrow-necked alembic stills are described as giving a delicate, clear spirit.
use: Bottled and labelled by hand; sold as Single Malt Nagahama and single cask releases; the brewery restaurant and the distillery sit next to JR Nagahama station.
craft: Scale is the point: a batch fills about one cask, so lots are tiny and cask-to-cask variation is expected. The yearly volume figure (about 80,000 litres) comes from one source only; treat it as indicative.

name: Kanosuke Distillery (Komasa Jozo)
text: Whisky distillery of the shochu maker Komasa Jozo, on the Fukiagehama coast in Hioki, Kagoshima; the new whisky licence dates to 2017. It runs three pot stills of different shapes and ages part of its spirit in casks that previously held long-aged shochu (the 'Mellow Kozuru' casks). Part of the barley is Kagoshima 'Hoshun' barley, malted locally. Diageo invested in 2021 and the single malt won gold at the 2023 International Spirits Challenge.
flavor: The maker describes a rich, sweet spirit; shochu-cask influence is described as gentle sweetness, mint and umeshu-like Japanese notes.
use: Single Malt Kanosuke (including a Kagoshima-only 48% bottling); also sold through lottery at retail.
craft: One explanation holds that a fermentation that grows lactic acid bacteria fast suppresses the metallic note that young spirit tends to show; this is a secondary account, so confirm with the distillery. Founding year and still details differ between blogs and the maker.

name: Saburomaru Distillery (Wakatsuru Shuzo)
ja: 三郎丸蒸留所（若鶴酒造）
text: Distillery of the sake brewery Wakatsuru Shuzo in Toyama, the only whisky distillery in Hokuriku. It obtained its whisky licence in 1952, stopped for a period and resumed in July 2017. Re-equipment was funded by crowdfunding of 38 million yen, about 75% from local backers. Sake is brewed in winter and whisky distilled in summer. It is known for peated, smoky malt and for a cast-iron pot still reported in 2019 as the world's first cast still.
flavor: Smoky, peated style is its stated specialty.
use: Sold as Saburomaru single malt and related bottlings; a retailer lists very small annual output (about 25 casks).
craft: The seasonal split (sake in winter, whisky in summer) shapes the production calendar. The cast-iron still ('ZEMON') claim was only partly visible in the sources, so cite it as reported rather than verified.

name: Sakurao Distillery (Chugoku Jozo, Hatsukaichi)
text: Distillery of Chugoku Jozo (founded 1918) at Sakurao, Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima. The company stopped whisky in 1989 once imported whisky spread, and opened the present distillery in 2017 (2018 in some sources). Centrepiece is a German Holstein hybrid still; accounts differ on whether it is stainless with a copper column. Malt is peated and unpeated. Maturation is at Sakurao and in a disused rail tunnel at Togouchi, Akiota. Also makes Sakurao Gin from Hiroshima botanicals.
flavor: Not given in the sources; the hybrid still is presented as giving a layered, complex aroma.
use: Whisky and gin; the 'Sakurao Gin Limited' uses 100% Hiroshima botanicals: lemon, navel orange, yuzu, daidai, hinoki, oyster shell and Miyajima red pine.
craft: Hybrid still means pot and column functions in one rig, a design said to draw on shochu know-how. Verify opening year (2017 vs 2018) and still material before quoting.
src: West JR Temite - Sakurao Brewery and Distillery

name: Yasato Distillery (Kiuchi Brewery, Ishioka)
text: Kiuchi Brewery (founded 1823, maker of Hitachino Nest) began whisky in 2016 at its Nukata brewery and opened Yasato Distillery in Ishioka in 2020, in a renovated former community hall. Two Forsyths pot stills with narrow necks and downward-angled arms, for a heavier, grain-forward spirit. Four wooden washbacks: two oak (Slavonian and French) and two French acacia. Stated capacity is 300,000 litres a year, about 4,000 casks. Brand: Hinomaru Whisky.
flavor: Wooden washbacks are said to give a wash that is both weighty and fruity.
use: Hinomaru Whisky releases, including bottlings finished in Islay-malt casks and casks with sakura (cherry wood) heads.
craft: Mash tun and lauter tun are separate, a choice credited to Kiuchi's brewing since 1996. Casks are bourbon, sherry and red wine, plus imported casks refitted with cherry-wood heads. Malting at Ishioka and local grain were described as plans.

name: Niigata Kameda Distillery
text: Niigata small distillery making single malt from barley malt only. Equipment: two Forsyths pot stills. Process water is Agano River underflow. The house aim is a fruity, light spirit. Niigata-grown 'Yukihana Rokujo' barley is named as an intended raw material, but one source says current products mainly use Scottish barley, so check the batch.
flavor: Fruity and light, per the maker's stated aim.
use: Single malt including new-born (new make) bottlings such as 'Niigata Kameda New Born 2 years' at 55%, and a peated new-born.
craft: Verify barley origin per release: local-barley intent and imported-barley practice are both reported. Young bottlings of 2 years are sold as 'new born', not as aged whisky.

name: Yoshida Denzai Distillery (grain whisky, Murakami)
text: A distillery in Murakami, Niigata, that specialises in grain whisky, which is rare in Japan. It uses corn, rye and other grains; product examples use Hokkaido dent corn as the main grain. Grain whisky is generally milder than malt. Retail listings link it with the Niigata small-scale distillery company (Niigata Kameda), so the two names appear together; verify which entity made a given bottle.
flavor: Described as pure, transparent new make that is aged to amber; grain style is mild.
use: Sold as young grain new make with a peated option; a Niigata Nippo feature covers the distillery.
craft: A grain-only house is useful to blenders who need a local grain component. Details of still type and capacity were not in the sources, so they are left out.
src: Sake no Matsuzawa - Kameda Newborn Peated

name: Nikka Coffey Grain and Coffey Malt (Miyagikyo Coffey stills)
ja: ニッカ カフェグレーン／カフェモルト
text: Nikka runs Coffey continuous stills at the Miyagikyo distillery. They were already outdated when installed in the early 1960s; Taketsuru Masataka chose them because they leave grain flavour in the spirit. Another source says the first unit went in at Nishinomiya in 1963 and was moved to Miyagikyo in 1999; two Coffey stills stand at Miyagikyo, one renewed. Mainly corn for Coffey Grain; barley malt for Coffey Malt; also Coffey Gin and Coffey Vodka.
flavor: Sweet grain aroma, creamy body and gentle sweetness, unlike neutral modern grain whisky.
use: Grain component for blends and bottled as Nikka Coffey Grain and Nikka Coffey Malt.
craft: Less efficient and needs skilled operation compared with modern continuous stills, because congeners carry through and must be turned into pleasant grain character by technique.

name: Japanese Whisky labelling standard (2021)
ja: ジャパニーズウイスキーの表示基準
text: Voluntary standard published by the Japan Spirits and Liqueurs Makers Association on 16 February 2021. 'Japanese whisky' must use malted grain, grain and water collected in Japan; saccharification, fermentation and distillation must be in a Japanese distillery; the spirit must age at least 3 years in wooden casks of 700 litres or less in Japan. Names, place names, flags and era names that evoke Japan are restricted unless the label makes clear they do not apply. It is an industry rule, not in the tax law. Start date reports differ: April 2021 with a grace period to 31 March 2024, or April 2024.
flavor: Rule term; not a flavour.
use: Read it when judging a bottle labelled 'Japanese whisky'; world blends with imported whisky must not use Japan-evoking names.
craft: Check cask size (700 L or under), three years' ageing in Japan and the origin of the raw materials; a pre-2024 bottle may fall under the grace period.
src: Nikkei - Definition drafted by industry group

name: Muscat Bailey A
ja: マスカット・ベーリーA
text: Red grape bred by Kawakami Zenbei at Iwanohara Vineyard, Niigata (vineyard founded 1890). A cross of American Bailey with European Muscat Hamburg, usually dated to 1927, first fruiting 1931 and released 1940; sources vary. Kawakami made over 10,000 crosses and registered 22 varieties. Bred for the humid climate, resistant to powdery mildew and downy mildew and to cold and wet. Second to Koshu in Japanese wine-grape area, mainly in Yamanashi and Yamagata. OIV-listed in 2013.
flavor: Strawberry and candy aroma with a foxy character linked to furaneol; low tannin, light to medium body, fruity.
use: Light reds, rose, sparkling; also eaten fresh.
craft: Low tannin and strong sweet-fruit aroma suit light styles; oak and extraction change character. Years of crossing and release differ by source.

name: Yamasachi (Ikeda, Tokachi wine grape)
text: Cold-hardy red wine grape bred by the Ikeda Town Grape and Wine Research Institute, Hokkaido. Work began in 1978; it descends from 'Kiyomi' (a clone selected from the French hybrid Seibel 13053, 1969) crossed with native mountain grape (yamabudo). Cold and frost tolerance mean the vines need no winter burial, which cuts labour. Sister variety: Kiyomai. Listed by the OIV in November 2020. Sources vary on Kiyomi's parentage.
flavor: Herbaceous, wild-fruit aroma from the yamabudo parent, with strong acidity.
use: Red wine of Tokachi Wine; also gift and tax-donation sets.
craft: Strong acid and herbal profile; the viticultural gain is skipping burial of vines in Tokachi's severe winters.
src: Tokachi General Subprefectural Bureau - Tokachi wine

name: Kerner (Hokkaido, Yoichi)
text: White grape bred in 1929 at a Württemberg institute from the black grape Trollinger and Riesling, named for the poet-physician Justinus Kerner. German plantings peaked in 1992 and were about 2,032 ha in 2022. Seedlings reached Hokkaido from Germany in 1973 and it is now Hokkaido's largest white wine grape. Popular in Yoichi. Ripens late, mid to late September.
flavor: More body than Riesling with softer acidity and aromatic fruit.
use: Dry whites, also sparkling and late-harvest; bottled by Hokkaido wineries including Yoichi estates.
craft: Late ripening needs a long season; plantings are matched to cool zones. Local area figures for Hokkaido or Yoichi were not found in the sources.

name: Delaware (wine and table grape, Yamagata and Yamanashi)
text: American natural hybrid named in 1855 at Delaware, Ohio, introduced to Japan in 1872. The seedless table form depends on gibberellin: Yamanashi's fruit research station succeeded with seedless Delaware in 1959. Yamagata's Okitama area is the leading Delaware region, and in Takahata growers increasingly skip gibberellin and keep seeds for wine, which saves labour. Yamanashi is second in prefectural area for the variety.
flavor: Sweet, foxy, light; wine versions are fresh and easy.
use: Table grape and wine, including seeded fruit for wine in Takahata.
craft: Seedless treatment is a hormone step; seeded fruit for wine avoids it. Production figures for wine use were not in the sources.

name: Yamagata Wine (Kaminoyama, Nanyo, Takahata)
text: Yamagata wine history: the first Tohoku winery, Sakai Winery, opened in Akayu, Nanyo in 1892, and Takeda Winery in Kaminoyama began wine in 1920. One article counts 14 wineries, six in Murayama and six in Okitama. Kaminoyama, a basin with large day-night swings, is known for early European varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Chardonnay. Takahata Winery (1990) is the largest in Tohoku, and its contract farmers are said to grow about 10% of Japan's Chardonnay. Yamagata holds a wine GI.
flavor: Basin climate gives concentrated fruit; Takahata Bordeaux-style reds are meant for long ageing.
use: Cabernet and Merlot reds, Chardonnay, Delaware whites; winery visits with hot springs.
craft: Winery counts and the Chardonnay share are from one article and can date; confirm before citing.

name: Japan Wine and wine GI (Yamanashi, Hokkaido, Nagano, Yamagata, Osaka)
ja: 日本ワイン・地理的表示（GI）
text: 'Japan Wine' (nihon wine) is wine made from Japan-grown grapes, set apart from 'kokusan wine'. GI Yamanashi (July 2013) was Japan's first wine GI: grapes only from Yamanashi, brewed, stored and bottled in the prefecture, with stricter production standards from June 2017. GI Hokkaido was second (grapes only from Hokkaido). Nagano, Yamagata and Osaka were designated together later, making five. The 2015 NTA labelling notice sets thresholds such as 85% for a named variety.
flavor: Rule term; used when reading labels.
use: Check label for variety, harvest place and GI when choosing domestic wine for a list.
craft: The 85% threshold applies to variety and place claims under the notice. Year of the three-prefecture designation was not clear in the sources.
src: Tokyo Regional Taxation Bureau - GI Yamanashi

name: Hitachino Nest Beer (Kiuchi Brewery)
ja: 常陸野ネストビール（木内酒造）
text: Craft beer of Kiuchi Brewery, a sake maker in Naka, Ibaraki, founded in 1823 (maker of Kikumori). After the 1994 tax revision cut the minimum beer volume from 2,000 kL to 60 kL, the first Hitachino Nest was brewed in 1996 at the head brewery. 'Nest' comes from Kounosu, the place name, and from owls nesting in a garden tree. The Nukata brewery took over beer production in 2008; Korea and Hong Kong operations followed (Hong Kong 2016).
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Exported widely; Kiuchi also makes shochu, umeshu, wine and, since 2016, whisky.
craft: The company brings sake and beer brewing under one house; its Yasato distillery re-uses brewing practice (separate mash and lauter tuns).

name: Yo-Ho Brewing (Yona Yona Ale, Karuizawa)
ja: ヤッホーブルーイング（よなよなエール）
text: Ale brewery in Karuizawa, Nagano. Its own site says it was founded in 1996; Yona Yona Ale is dated 1997 in many sources and the company profile gives 1997. Early investment came from Hoshino Yoshiharu and the first brewery was in the Hoshino area. Yona Yona Ale is built on Cascade hops and ester-driven citrus aroma. 'Indo no Aooni' IPA was limited-run before becoming permanent in 2013; output rose six times from 2013 to 2020.
flavor: Citrus-like hop aroma and fruity esters (Yona Yona Ale); hop bitterness (IPA).
use: Sold widely in convenience stores and supermarkets.
craft: Hop-forward style meant to be drinkable at home; the foundation year differs (1996 vs 1997), so state both.

name: COEDO Beniaka (sweet potato beer, Kawagoe)
ja: コエドビール 紅赤
text: COEDO brand of Kyodo Shoji, named after 'Koedo', Kawagoe's nickname. Beniaka uses Kawagoe sweet potatoes, an idea from the mid-1990s to use discarded non-standard potatoes; it was the first commercial beer. The brewery opened 1996 and the craft-beer brand was set in 2006. Because of the sweet potato, it counts as happoshu under tax law. Switched from lager to ale in 2015. Won a 2008 Ag-Commerce-Industry 88 selection and a silver at the 2010 World Beer Cup. 'World first' is the company's own claim.
flavor: Not described in the sources.
use: Regional ingredient beer; sold across Japan.
craft: Wikipedia puts the brewery at Higashimatsuyama, not Kawagoe; one source says the original plan was local wheat before the potato.

name: Minoh Beer
text: Craft brewery in Minoh, Osaka. It grew from a liquor store: the founder's father said in 1996 he would make beer, taking up the 1994 deregulation, and brewing began in 1997. The current head, Oshita Kaori, has been head brewer since the start. It survived the collapse of the early jibiru boom. Product names were not covered by the sources used.
flavor: Not described in the sources consulted.
use: Sold as regional craft beer in the Kansai area.
craft: A useful example of a boom-era brewery that outlasted the early jibiru wave.

name: Baird Brewing (Numazu and Shuzenji)
ja: ベアードブルーイング
text: Founded in 2000 in Numazu, Shizuoka by American Bryan Baird and his wife Sayuri, starting from a 30-litre brewing tank. Beer sales began at a Numazu fish market taproom around 2001. In 2014 brewing and headquarters moved to Izu City, where the Brewery Garden Shuzenji by the Kano River has large 6,000-litre tanks, a farm and a campsite. The operator is Baird Brewing, a limited partnership. Sources disagree on the Numazu address.
flavor: Not described in the sources.
use: Taproom and brewery tours at Shuzenji; sold nationwide.
craft: Pioneer craft brewer in Japan; the Shuzenji site shows a farm-factory model.

name: Ise Kadoya Brewery (Nikenchaya Mochi Kadoya)
text: Beer arm of Nikenchaya Mochi Kadoya Honten in Ise, a rice-cake shop said to date to 1575. Miso and soy brewing began in 1923, and in 1997 the 21st head, Suzuki Narimune, started beer, partly to revive 'Shinto Mugishu', an English-style ale made in Ise for five years from 1887. The first beer was Pale Ale (5.0%, IBU 35, Cascade hops). Pale Ale won gold at the International Brewing Awards in 2017; another site lists 2017, 2019, 2021 and 2024.
flavor: Fruity, with flowery Cascade aroma.
use: Pale Ale is the flagship; also West Coast Pilsner.
craft: The head's name in 1923 is given as Suzuki Kasuke or Suzuki Tokichi depending on the source.

name: Orion Beer (Nago, Okinawa)
text: Okinawa Beer Co. was set up on 18 May 1957 in Nago under US administration; the name Orion was chosen from about 2,500 public entries and sales began in 1959, when the company took the name. Draft beer arrived in 1960. Its one plant is in Nago and uses Yanbaru water. The Draft uses Ie Island barley. Cooling plant took about a year and a half to install. Premium products were developed using yeast found in Okinawa from about 3,000 samples. Listed on the Tokyo Prime market on 25 September 2025.
flavor: Clean, easy drinking, suited to hot weather.
use: Okinawa's local beer.
craft: Some figures, such as local market share of about 60%, were not backed in sources.

name: Otaru Beer
text: Beer from the Otaru canal, Hokkaido. The brew pub 'Otaru Warehouse No.1' opened in July 1995 in a canal grain warehouse, run by Aleph (the Bikkuri Donkey group); a second plant at Zenibako opened in 1999. It follows the 1516 German purity law: only water, malt, hops and yeast, with decoction mashing. Standard lines: Pilsner, Dunkel and Weiss.
flavor: Dunkel: roasted malt, caramel, toast and nut notes with strong malt sweetness.
use: German-style beers; Dunkel is a dark lager.
craft: Dunkel uses much caramel malt with double decoction in one account, which is from a blog.

name: Iwate Kura Beer (Sekinoichi Shuzo, Ichinoseki)
ja: いわて蔵ビール（世嬉の一酒造）
text: Beer of Sekinoichi Shuzo in Ichinoseki, Iwate, a sake brewery founded in 1918 as Yokoya Shuzo and renamed in 1957. Beer started in 1995 as a cooperative of five local companies; the licence and brew pub date to 1996 (pub opened December 1996), though one article says sales began in 1997. It brews with the same water as its sake and avoids filtration and pasteurisation. It has won World Beer Cup and World Beer Awards medals. In 2026 sake brewing was revived after 40 years.
flavor: Unfiltered, unpasteurised beer.
use: Brew pub and restaurant at the brewery, with a museum on site.
craft: Dates for beer start range from 1995 to 1997 across sources.

name: Sankt Gallen Brewery (Atsugi)
text: Brewery in Atsugi, Kanagawa, called an original jibiru pioneer. It dates to 1993 with brewing in San Francisco; it moved to Atsugi in 1997. Brewing stopped in 2001, the company was refounded in 2002 and brewing resumed in spring 2003. Imperial Chocolate Stout (2006) became a Valentine's hit; Shonan Gold was launched in 2008.
flavor: Imperial Chocolate Stout: dark and rich, chocolate-themed.
use: Seasonal Valentine release; taproom in Hon-Atsugi.
craft: The sources did not say whether Shonan Gold is organic.

name: Jibiru and the 1994 brewing deregulation
ja: 地ビール・1994年酒税法改正
text: In April 1994 the Liquor Tax Law was revised and the minimum annual beer production needed for a licence fell from 2,000 kL to 60 kL (happoshu 6 kL). The first licence went to a new operator in December 1994, and about 300 small breweries opened nationwide. The boom later cooled, and 200 or more brewers remain (date not stated). 'Jibiru' (local beer) was long used synonymously with craft beer in Japan.
flavor: Rule and history term.
use: Context for dating a brewery: pre-1994 means big maker, post-1994 means small licence.
craft: The 2,000 kL to 60 kL change is the figure to cite; counts of breweries vary by source and date.
src: National Association of Local Beer Brewers

name: Nikka Hirosaki Cidre (Hirosaki Plant)
ja: ニッカ弘前 生シードル
text: Often called the birthplace of Japanese cider. Asahi Cidre Co. started making cider in 1954 and launched 'Asahi Cidre' in 1956. In 1960 Nikka's Taketsuru Masataka was asked to take over; the Yoshino-cho plant is now the Hirosaki Museum of Contemporary Art brick warehouse. The present Sakae-cho plant was built in 1965, Nikka Cidre appeared in 1972, an unheated cidre in 1985 (regional) and nationwide in 1988. It was relaunched in 2023. It is 100% apple.
flavor: Apple character kept intact.
use: Sparkling apple wine based on French cidre but adjusted to Japanese taste.
craft: Non-heat-treated cidre is the key technical step of 1985.

name: Hirosaki Cidre Kobo kimori
text: Cider workshop inside the Apple Park in Hirosaki, founded in 2008 and run by young apple farmers who make the cider themselves. The name 'kimori' comes from the custom of leaving one apple on the tree after harvest as thanks and a prayer for next year's crop. The dry cider is crisp, with apple flavour. The workshop serves glasses on a terrace beside the orchard.
flavor: Dry, clean, apple-forward.
use: Drink on site or bottle.
craft: Grower-made cider; the dry version keeps the apple flavour.

name: Nagano Cidre (Iizuna, Matsukawa, Ina)
text: Nagano's appellation system certifies cider made from 100% Nagano apples and brewed in the prefecture. Ringo Gakko Brewery in Iizuna took its fruit-wine licence in February 2019, uses 1,000, 500 and 220 litre tanks and sells 'Gakkyu' ciders by variety and harvest period (classes 1-5). Its owner Ono Tsukasa founded the Japan Cidre Masters Association in 2015. Others: Marukame (Matsukawa), Takayashiro Farm (Nakano, winery from 2004), Kamoshika Cidre (Ina).
flavor: Dry versions are common; honey-yeast bottle fermentation is claimed for one product.
use: Pair with local food; many makers.
craft: Variety-by-variety vinification mirrors harvest timing.

name: Umaji Village Yuzu-shu
text: Liqueurs and spirits made from yuzu from Umaji, Kochi. Home method: yuzu, rock sugar and shochu steeped about three months. Commercial forms: Kozaemon Yuzushu (Nakajima Jozo), 100% Umaji yuzu juice on a junmai sake base at 6.5%; Onikoroshi Yuzushu (Kiyosu Sakura), Umaji juice with brewing alcohol, sugar and acidulant at 8%; Umajimura Yuzushu, domestic gin with Umaji juice at 17-18%; and Shinozaki's yuzu-umeshu blending umeshu, juice and ponkan juice.
flavor: Sweet and tangy citrus.
use: Neat, on the rocks or diluted.
craft: Base spirit decides strength and style: sake, brewing alcohol or gin.

name: Wakayama Umeshu (GI) and Nakano BC Kishu Umeshu
ja: 和歌山梅酒・中野BC紀州梅酒
text: Wakayama Umeshu was the first liqueur to get a GI. Standards: ume (green or fully ripe) harvested in Wakayama, with steeping through storage and filling done in the prefecture. Nakano BC uses only Nankoume from contract growers, steeped soon after harvest, with a dedicated umeshu toji, said to be the only one in Japan. It stirs only the liquid by pump to protect the fruit and steeps in stages. Strengths run from 12 to 20%. Home rule: 1 kg ume to 1.8 L, base spirit at 20% or more.
flavor: Fruity ume character.
use: Neat, on ice or diluted.
craft: Under tax law, steeping spirit under 20% is treated as new manufacture; only ume, sugar and 20%+ alcohol are allowed, and small herbs may be tolerated.
src: Kishu Baien - how to make umeshu

name: Kyoto Craft Uji Tea Liqueur
ja: 京都クラフト宇治茶リキュール
text: A Kyoto Prefecture project: Liquor Mountain, bartenders, tea masters and sake makers developed an Uji tea liqueur using 100% Uji tea, testing three Uji teas. They approached Sasaki Shuzo, which holds a liqueur licence. MAFF defines Uji tea as tea from Kyoto, Nara, Shiga and Mie finished by Kyoto firms using Uji-derived methods; types include tencha, sencha, gyokuro and hojicha.
flavor: Uji tea aroma; details not given.
use: Bar and cocktail use.
craft: Tea choice per lot was tested by trial with tea masters.
src: Kyoto Prefecture - Craft Uji Tea Liqueur

name: Myo-CHA Tea Liqueurs (Rikyugura, Sakai) incl. Hojicha
text: Sake brewery Rikyugura, in Sakai, Osaka, the only brewery in Sakai, makes sake-based tea liqueurs named after the wife of Sen no Rikyu. Lines: matcha, sakura-matcha and hojicha, at 8% alcohol, with no added colour or flavour. The sakura-matcha uses 100% Uji matcha; the hojicha uses Yame tea from Kyushu. The company name is given as Rikyugura Ltd. in one source and as kabushiki-kaisha elsewhere.
flavor: Natural tea sweetness.
use: Served cold or diluted.
craft: Yame hojicha supplies the roast note.

name: Ramune (marble-stoppered soda, Hata Kosen)
text: Carbonated drink in a Codd-neck bottle sealed by a marble, the stopper devised by Hiram Codd (patents in Britain 1872 and the US 1873; reaching Japan around 1887 by one account). Tokunaga Tamakichi of Osaka is credited with perfecting the bottle in Japan. The name derives from 'lemonade'. At Hata Kosen in Osaka, syrup and carbonated water are filled, the bottle capped and inverted so gas pressure seats the marble. To open, press the plunger and hold it 5-6 seconds. 'Bi-dama' may come from 'A-dama' or 'bidoro'.
flavor: Sweet, fizzy lemon-style soda.
use: Summer soft drink and festival item.
craft: Pink plunger means screw cap, green or clear means driven stopper. MAFF defines ramune as a carbonated drink in a marble ramune bottle.
src: Hata Kosen - how ramune is made

name: Arima Cider Teppo-sui (Arima Onsen)
ja: 有馬サイダー てっぽう水
text: Arima's carbonated spring was once called poison water. A town head, Kajiki Genjiro, had it analysed (1873 or 1875 by source). Arima Kosen began bottled carbonated water in 1901 under a cannon-like label named teppo (gun) after its popping cork, and sweetened cider came in 1908. In 1926 production moved to Hirano, Kawanishi; at Hirano, bottled water had started in 1884. Local volunteers revived it in 2002 as 'Arima Cider' through Arima Hasuke Shoten. The old recipe is lost, so it is not an exact reproduction.
flavor: Very strong carbonation with refined sweetness.
use: Souvenir drink.
craft: The revival changed the recipe from the original.

name: Ji-saida (regional cider boom)
text: Ji-saida or go-tochi saida are sodas made by small local firms. The Japan Soft Drink Association counts 51 brands before 2005 and 158 in 2011. The 2002 relaunch of Arima Cider is credited with reviving local mineral-water makers and reissues. One source dates Japan's first domestic cider to 1868 Yokohama ('champagne cider'). In Taisho Tokyo, firms made Kagetsu-jirushi and Kimigayo cider; Tokyo Cider was reissued in Sumida.
flavor: Local sodas, often stronger in carbonation.
use: Souvenir and gift soda.
craft: Check the maker: local mineral-water works, not national brands such as Mitsuya.
src: Japan Soft Drinks Association - soft drink history

name: Hoppy (Tokyo beer-taste mixer)
text: Beer-taste drink launched in July 1948 in postwar Tokyo, first named 'Hobby' and changed to Hoppy. The maker's predecessor, Shusuisha, made ramune and cider (founded 1910 per one source, 1905 per another). Development reportedly began in 1926, taking 22 years, and a patent followed in 1956. Black Hoppy, from four malts, began in 1992. Mixing it with shochu came from izakaya customers; 'naka' (shochu) and 'soto' arose among fans, not the maker.
flavor: Beer-like, light.
use: Poured over shochu, with 'naka' meaning the shochu glass.
craft: Company names changed (Kokka Inryo in 1948, later Hoppy Beverage); dates vary.

name: Inoda Coffee (Kyoto)
text: Kyoto coffee house founded in 1940 by Inoda Shichiro, first as a coffee wholesaler; it opened as a cafe after the war, one source saying seven years on. The signature blend is 'Arabia no Shinju', a Mocha-based dark-roast European-style blend served with sugar and milk already added. Coffee is made by craftsmen using nel drip. The main store's 'Kyo no Choshoku' breakfast started in 1994. The Sanjo store reopened in October 2024 with its oval counter intact.
flavor: Deep roast, rich and balanced.
use: Kyoto breakfast cafe.
craft: Nel drip lets through components paper would filter out.
src: Walker Plus - Inoda main store breakfast

name: Nishimura Coffee (Kobe)
text: Kobe coffee house founded in 1948 by Kawase Kiyoko as a three-table shop, first selling sweets and Japanese tea and adding coffee at customers' request; it moved to its present site in 1952. It says it first put straight coffee on the menu when blends dominated. Coffee is nel-dripped with Miyamizu from Nada, checked by the sake association. The Kitanozaka store opened in 1974 as a members-only cafe, until 1995.
flavor: Not described in the sources.
use: Kissaten coffee in a classic setting.
craft: 'Japan first' claims are from the shop's own sites and not independently confirmed.

name: Cafe de l'Ambre (Ginza)
ja: カフェ・ド・ランブル
text: Ginza coffee-only shop opened in 1948 by Sekiguchi Ichiro, who died in 2018 aged 103 after his film-equipment business failed. He is known for 'old coffee': green beans aged over ten years before roasting. First in a back alley of West Ginza; moved to Ginza 8-chome, dated to the 1970s by one source. Billed as a pioneer of Japanese in-house roasting.
flavor: Aged beans, mellow.
use: Coffee-only kissaten.
craft: Aged green beans are the signature.

name: Nagoya Morning (Ichinomiya origin)
text: The morning-set culture is said to start in Ichinomiya, Aichi, a textile town where traders met in cafes during the Gachaman boom. One shop added a boiled egg and peanuts to morning coffee; other shops followed and it spread to Nagoya. Other explanations: Owari's tea-ceremony tradition, and hospitality. Nagoya has many independent shops and meal menus.
flavor: Not applicable.
use: Set of coffee with toast or egg.
craft: There is no single agreed origin.

name: Kissaten and nel drip
ja: 喫茶店・ネルドリップ
text: Coffee reached Japan via Dejima; Ota Nanpo drank it in 1804. Cafe-style shops spread in the Taisho era, and coffee-only 'kissaten' were distinguished from the 1930s. Bean imports resumed in 1950 and instant coffee boomed from 1961. A domestic siphon appeared in 1925. A kissaten boom ran 1965-83 with up to about 180,000 shops. Nel drip uses a flannel filter that passes more components than paper.
flavor: Nel drip: fuller extraction than paper.
use: Used on cafe menus.
craft: Flannel filters need care.
